method: Local editorial king-of-the-hill tournament; these are self-assessments, not make.fun judge verdicts or external model calls.
rubric: Each criterion is scored from 1 (weak) to 10 (strong). Totals guide comparisons; surprise, clarity, economy, and a concrete human reaction break close decisions.

candidates.subject: stapler
candidates.text: I asked my stapler to hold my life together. It said it could do twenty sheets, not thirty-seven years. I bought the heavy-duty model.

candidates.subject: umbrella
candidates.text: I asked my umbrella to keep a low profile. It opened on the bus and introduced me to everyone. I got off two stops early.

candidates.subject: coffee maker
candidates.text: I asked my coffee maker to help me get through Monday. It handed me a passport and forty dollars. I asked if we could afford to bring the dog.

candidates.subject: houseplant
candidates.text: I asked my houseplant to show a little gratitude. It grew toward my neighbor's window. I closed the blinds and called it quality time.

candidates.subject: electric toothbrush
candidates.text: I asked my electric toothbrush for a gentler setting. It sent me a video titled 'Brushing Without Your Mum.' I watched the whole thing.

candidates.subject: pressure cooker
candidates.text: I asked my pressure cooker how it handles stress. It said, 'I let off steam. You send thirteen voice notes.' I deleted the group chat.

candidates.subject: reusable water bottle
candidates.text: I asked my reusable water bottle why it cost forty dollars. It said it came with a personality. I carried it to a meeting and waited.

candidates.subject: suitcase
candidates.text: I asked my suitcase why it wouldn't close. It said, 'You are not going to read six novels in three days.' I took out the underwear.

candidates.subject: phone autocorrect
candidates.text: My phone's autocorrect changed 'I love you' to 'I owe you' — my girlfriend replied 'knew it' before I could explain the typo.

candidates.subject: printer
candidates.text: My printer only works when I threaten it out loud, which is why my will now includes a clause about the printer.

candidates.subject: dishwasher
candidates.text: I asked my dishwasher to stop judging how I load it. It printed a seating chart for six plates and put me at the kids' table.

candidates.subject: label maker
candidates.text: I asked my label maker to organize the house. It printed 'GUEST' for my side of the bed. My wife laminated it.

candidates.subject: desk fan
candidates.text: I told my desk fan I felt ignored. It turned away halfway through. I waited for it to come back before finishing the story.

candidates.subject: TV remote
candidates.text: I asked my TV remote to help me find a connection. It paired with the neighbor's television. I turned the volume up so they'd know I was happy for it.

candidates.subject: kettle
candidates.text: I asked my kettle why it screams every morning. It said, 'You get to leave.' I started taking it to work.

candidates.subject: doormat
candidates.text: I told my doormat I felt taken for granted. It said, 'You get to go inside.' I brought it in and stood outside to think.

matches.reason: The heavy-duty purchase exposes recognizable denial; getting off a bus is a more predictable embarrassment response.
Equal totals, but the passport, forty dollars, and dog produce a stranger escalation than the familiar life-together metaphor.
Actual plant behavior grounds the absurdity; the narrator's controlling response lands more cleanly than the coffee maker's unexplained escape supplies.
Closing the blinds creates a sharper character reveal than watching an instructional video.
The plant's visual betrayal and the narrator's petty punishment are less familiar than letting-off-steam wordplay.
The plant has a clearer action and consequence; waiting for a bottle's personality is a quieter anticlimax.
Six novels in three days makes the criticism concrete; sacrificing underwear instead of a book adds an independent second surprise and self-own.
The seed's love/owe substitution is familiar and its explanation trails the laugh; the suitcase ends directly on the absurd human choice.
The printer seed has an excellent inheritance escalation, but an unspecified clause is less visual than discarding underwear to preserve a doomed reading plan.
The suitcase's refusal has a physical cause and its owner supplies the kicker; the dishwasher needs a more invented seating-chart mechanism.
Close: lamination is an economical human reaction, but a wife rejecting her husband is a more familiar destination than choosing six novels over clean underwear.
Closest match: the oscillating fan is highly relatable, but waiting follows its mechanical motion; removing underwear reverses the suitcase's advice in a less expected way.
The remote extends a familiar pairing-as-romance analogy; the suitcase needs fewer words and ends on a stronger physical detail.
The kettle has a sympathetic ending, but the suitcase's self-sabotage is a sharper laugh than an act of kindness.
The doormat's role reversal is gently absurd; the suitcase keeps a more recognizable motive and a more specific final image.

selection_reason: A mundane packing problem, a brutally specific prediction, and a human who protects the fantasy instead of the underwear: three clear beats with the most concrete word saved for last.

revision_after_first_run.change: Replaced 'You are not going to' with 'You won't'; the first run was read back before editing main.py a second time.
revision_after_first_run.final_text: I asked my suitcase why it wouldn't close. It said, 'You won't read six novels in three days.' I took out the underwear.
revision_after_first_run.reason: Eleven fewer characters; a more conversational rebuke; the concrete human kicker is unchanged.
